late-036.title: Out of Africa along the Southern Route
late-036.text: Almost everyone whose family roots lie outside Africa descends from one small band of travelers. People outside Africa today come mainly from a single expansion of Homo sapiens, about 70,000 to 50,000 years ago. A small group carrying the maternal lineage called mitochondrial haplogroup L3, perhaps fewer than 1,000 people, crossed the Bab-el-Mandeb strait into Arabia. From there they followed the coasts. They worked their way around Arabia and Persia and reached South Asia before 55,000 years ago. Their descendants pressed on toward Southeast Asia and Oceania. Not everyone kept to the shore. Around 50,000 years ago, others entered Eurasia through the Zagros Mountains, and some headed for the steppes of Central Asia. The expansion had a shadow. Extinctions driven by humans began as people spread out of Africa over 60,000 years ago.

late-035.title: Lake Lisan fills the Jordan Rift
late-035.text: A great lake once filled a deep valley in the Near East. Lake Lisan filled the Jordan Rift Valley in West Asia from about 70,000 to 12,000 years ago, through most of the Last Glacial Period.

late-038.title: The first people reach Australia
late-038.text: Reaching Australia meant crossing open sea. People moved from Sunda, the Asian shelf, through the islands of Wallacea to Sahul, the joined landmass of Australia and New Guinea. They had followed the southern coast of Asia to get there. Madjedbebe in northern Australia was possibly occupied by 65,000 ± 6,000 years ago, and at least by 50,000. The older date is disputed. A 2020 study suggested termites had disturbed the layers, and 50,000 years has long been the accepted figure. Settlement of southern Australia came during a wet period between 60,000 and 40,000 years ago.

late-039.title: Modern humans mix with Neanderthals and Denisovans
late-039.text: Leaving Africa did not mean leaving other humans behind. Migrants interbred with archaic people already living outside it, adding their DNA to the modern gene pool. An earlier modern wave had exchanged genes with Neanderthals around 100,000 years ago. Linkage studies date the last Neanderthal gene flow into the ancestors of Europeans to 47,000 to 65,000 years ago. Denisovan genes entered the ancestors of Oceanians after they split from Eurasians, about 50,000 years ago, and before 37,000 years ago. Tianyuan man, who lived in China about 40,000 years ago, carried substantial Neanderthal ancestry.

late-040.title: A brief modern human visit to Mandrin Cave
late-040.text: In layer E of Mandrin Cave, in France's Rhône valley, lie modern human teeth, including a baby's molar, and stone tools of a style called Neronian. They date to 56,800 to 51,700 years ago. The layers just below and above hold Neanderthal remains and Mousterian tools. The two peoples' stays may have been only years apart. The tools resemble finds at Ksar Akil in Lebanon, suggesting a brief incursion from the Levant. Jean-Jacques Hublin says that idea remains to be confirmed.

late-041.title: The last Denisovans
late-041.text: The Denisovans fade from view slowly. In the Altai cave that gave them their name, the Denisova 3 finger bone dates to 76,200 to 51,600 years ago, and they are confirmed there only until about 55,000 years ago. Further south, Denisovan mitochondrial DNA in the sediments of the cave that held the Xiahe jaw spans 100,000 to 60,000 years ago, perhaps later. A Denisovan rib fragment from Baishiya Cave, China, is younger still, at 48,000 to 32,000 years ago.

late-043.title: The Flores hobbit vanishes
late-043.text: The small human of Flores lasted until the newcomers came. Homo floresiensis, nicknamed the 'Hobbit', lived on the island until modern humans arrived about 50,000 years ago. Its bones at Liang Bua date from 100,000 to 60,000 years ago, and its youngest stone tools are about 50,000 years old. Its world was already under strain. A drying trend intensified around 61,000 years ago, shrinking fresh water and the dwarf elephant relative it may have hunted. Bones of that animal, Stegodon florensis, lie at Liang Bua with Hobbit tools, a few bearing cut marks. The dwarf Stegodon's last records also date to about 50,000 years ago, around the time modern humans reached Flores.

late-044.title: Homo luzonensis, a small human of the Philippines
late-044.text: A few teeth and finger bones in Callao Cave revealed a new kind of human on Luzon. Homo luzonensis was small, possibly a pygmy form. Described in 2019, the fossils indicate it lived on the island between 50,000 and 67,000 years ago. Hominins had been active on Luzon far earlier, as early as 771,000 to 631,000 years ago.

late-045.title: The last giant python-like snakes
late-045.text: Australia was the last home of an ancient line of snakes. Madtsoiids, giant primitive python-like snakes such as Wonambi, survived there until about 50,000 years ago.

late-046.title: The great megafauna die-off begins
late-046.text: From around 50,000 years ago, most of the large land animals outside Africa died out. The extinction was unprecedented for one reason: it struck the biggest species hardest. About 65% of megafaunal species vanished worldwide. The toll was 72% in North America, 83% in South America and 88% in Australia. The timing tracked people. Losses began in Sahul about 50,000 years ago and in the Americas about 13,000 years ago, each as modern humans arrived. Africa was hit less than other continents. Hunting, climate change or both are blamed. Scientists still argue over the balance, though most accept that humans played at least some part. The damage lasts. Mammal diversity lost since then could take 5 to 7 million years to recover.

late-047.title: Meteor Crater blasted into Arizona
late-047.text: About 50,000 years ago, a nickel-iron meteorite about 50 m across slammed into the Colorado Plateau and blasted out Meteor Crater. The land was cooler and damper then: open grassland and woods where mammoths and giant ground sloths roamed. It is called the best-preserved meteorite crater on Earth.

late-048.title: The Rotoiti eruption in New Zealand
late-048.text: About 50,000 years ago, New Zealand's Ōkataina caldera erupted at Rotoiti. It left ignimbrite and tephra spread over a wide area. Paired eruptions at Rotoiti and Earthquake Flat produced about 120 km³ and 10 km³ of material.

late-042.title: Procoptodon, the giant short-faced kangaroo
late-042.text: The largest kangaroo known stood about 2 m tall and weighed up to 240 kg. Procoptodon goliah may have been the largest hopping mammal ever. It died out about 50,000 to 45,000 years ago, though some evidence suggests it lasted until 18,000 years ago. Its loss came with the arrival of people, in a fairly stable climate. Hunting, burning of vegetation by people and drought have all been proposed. Which mattered most is debated.

late-049.title: The Upper Paleolithic: a burst of new tools and art
late-049.text: Before 50,000 years ago, stone tools looked much the same everywhere. Then artifacts became markedly more diverse. Africa's Middle Stone Age ended about then, and the Upper Paleolithic began between 50,000 and 40,000 years ago. Signs of modern behavior are unambiguous from 40,000 to 50,000 years ago. Whether this was a sudden 'Great Leap Forward' is debated. Art followed. Spanish cave paintings and the Lion-man figurine date to around 40,000 years ago. The Aurignacian culture flourished in Europe and southwest Asia from 43,000 to 26,000 years ago.

late-051.title: Topper and the disputed pre-Clovis claims
late-051.text: Charcoal at a chert quarry in South Carolina sparked a long argument. At Topper, charcoal lay below the Clovis layer, beside chipped chert read as tools, and was radiocarbon dated to about 50,000 years ago. Critics say the chert broke naturally and the charcoal came from a wildfire. They also note that 50,000 years is the limit of radiocarbon dating. Others still cite Topper as a pre-Clovis site, but about 16,000 years old.

late-050.title: Genyornis, the last of the giant dromornithid birds
late-050.text: Genyornis newtoni stood 2 to 2.5 m tall and could not fly. By the Late Pleistocene it was the only surviving dromornithid, a family that had been diverse in the Miocene. It lived until around 50,000 to 40,000 years ago. At Lake Callabonna its population died about 50,000 years ago as the lake dried up. Burned eggshells 53,900 to 43,400 years old suggest people collected and cooked its eggs before it vanished. Drying lakes and human predation are both proposed causes, and the debate is unresolved.

late-052.title: Australia loses its giants
late-052.text: Every mammal over 1,000 kg on the Australian mainland disappeared. All forms of megafauna there died out in the same rapid window, about 46,000 years ago, considerably earlier than on other continents. The victims included Diprotodon, the largest marsupial known, and the giant monitor lizard Megalania. Diprotodon was last recorded at South Walker Creek about 40,100 years ago. A Zygomaturus from New South Wales, 33,000 to 37,000 years old, is the latest known survivor. The losses followed human arrival rather than any known climate shift. Climate then resembled today's, and drying is judged an unlikely cause. Still, how much people contributed remains controversial.

late-053.title: Fire-stick farming reshapes Australia
late-053.text: Australians were shaping their land with fire 46,000 years ago. Ash in the Coral Sea shows fire was already significant there over 100,000 years ago. About 45,000 years ago fire becomes abruptly more common. One geologist attributed the rise to Aboriginal fire-stick farming, the deliberate burning of forests and grasslands. One account holds that dense forest turned into open forest and grassland, favoring eucalyptus, acacia and grasses. How far burning changed the vegetation, and whether it helped drive the megafauna extinctions, is debated.

late-054.title: Modern humans reach Flores
late-054.text: Teeth from Liang Bua cave, about 46,000 years old, probably belonged to Homo sapiens. They are the earliest evidence of modern humans on Flores. Stone tools from then on use different raw materials, so modern humans, not Homo floresiensis, likely made them. The newcomers arrived soon after the last records of the Hobbit and the dwarf Stegodon, around 50,000 years ago.

late-055.title: Modern humans reach Europe
late-055.text: Europe was settled by people who already knew how to hunt the big game of the cold steppe. Modern humans came from Central Asia and the Middle East. They had reached northwestern Europe by 45,000 years ago; remains in Germany date to 45,000 to 47,000 years ago. Finds in Italy and Britain date to 43,000 to 45,000 years ago, and by 45,000 years ago people lived as far north as 61° N. Even so, the continent stayed nearly empty. Settling it may have taken 15,000 to 20,000 years, and from 40,000 to 16,000 years ago it held only some 4,000 to 6,000 people. Most of their mixing with Neanderthals had ended before they arrived, by 47,000 years ago.

late-056.title: Modern humans push into Siberia and the Arctic
late-056.text: The remains of Ust'-Ishim man show modern humans in Siberia at 58° N by about 45,000 years ago. People entered the mammoth steppe and reached the Siberian Arctic around then. They reached Japan by about 30,000 years ago, and Siberia above the Arctic Circle by about 27,000 years ago.

late-057.title: The Châtelperronian, a Neanderthal toolkit
late-057.text: Curved-backed flint knives from France and Spain raise a question: did Neanderthals pick up new ideas? The Châtelperronian, about 44,500 to 33,000 years ago, was the earliest Upper Paleolithic industry in central and southwestern France and northern Spain. It is the only Upper Paleolithic industry credited to Neanderthals, perhaps copying modern human techniques. Both its reality and its makers are debated. Critics see it as a mix of Mousterian and Aurignacian layers.

late-058.title: The straight-tusked elephant's last stand
late-058.text: Its bulls averaged 4 m tall and 13 tonnes, among the largest land mammals ever. Palaeoloxodon antiquus, the straight-tusked elephant, retreated from northern Europe after the Last Interglacial ended about 115,000 years ago. It may have lingered in Britain until 87,000 years ago. Its youngest confirmed remains, from Iberia, are about 44,000 to 43,000 years old. Footprints may stretch its record to 28,000 years ago.

late-059.title: Ngwenya, the oldest known mine
late-059.text: About 43,000 years ago, people at Ngwenya in Eswatini dug hematite out of the ground to make red ochre, a pigment. It is the oldest mining known anywhere.

late-060.title: The Laschamp excursion: a brief magnetic flip
late-060.text: Between 42,200 and 41,500 years ago, Earth's magnetic field briefly reversed. The flip took about 250 years, and the field stayed reversed for about 440. In transition it fell to 5% of today's strength. With the shield weakened, more cosmic rays reached Earth. They raised the production of beryllium-10 and carbon-14, thinned the ozone layer and altered the circulation of the air. A fossil kauri tree from New Zealand, alive 42,500 to 41,000 years ago, recorded the event in its rings. Claimed links to the megafauna and Neanderthal extinctions, and to cave art, lack supporting evidence.

late-061.title: The Lake Mungo burials
late-061.text: Lake Mungo 1 was burned twice and then covered with ochre carried from hundreds of kilometers away. It is among the oldest known cremations. Human remains from Lake Mungo in southeastern Australia date to about 42,000 years ago. The Willandra Lakes then held deep fresh water, and people lived on their shores 40,000 to 35,000 years ago.

late-062.title: The Neanderthals disappear
late-062.text: About 40,000 years ago they disappeared from the fossil record, and their distinctive tools vanished with them. A 2021 recalibration dates their extinction to 40,700 ± 200 years ago. They had already vanished from northwestern Europe by 44,200 to 40,600 years ago. Modern humans spreading from Africa replaced them across Eurasia. Iberia was one of their last strongholds, with possible holdouts there 37,000 years ago. Another possible refuge was Byzovaya in the Urals, near the Arctic, about 33,000 to 32,000 years ago. They did not vanish entirely. A small amount of Neanderthal DNA survives in people today, a legacy of the interbreeding described in {{ref:late-039}}.

late-063.title: Walking to Tasmania
late-063.text: About 43,000 years ago, low glacial seas exposed the Bassian Plain, a land bridge from mainland Australia to Tasmania. People walked across about 40,000 years ago and became the Aboriginal Tasmanians. Tasmania's megafauna disappeared about 41,000 years ago, apparently through hunting.

late-064.title: The last marsupial lions
late-064.text: Australia's top predator was a marsupial. Thylacoleo, the 'pouch lion', lived from the late Pliocene until around 40,000 years ago. Since the Pliocene it had been the only surviving genus of its family, the Thylacoleonidae. It vanished at about the same time as most Australian megafauna. How much climate change or newly arrived people were to blame is debated.

late-065.title: The Campanian Ignimbrite eruption near Naples
late-065.text: The largest eruption in the history of the Campi Flegrei, near Naples, came from the Archiflegreo volcano. Argon–argon dating puts it at 39,850 ± 140 years ago. It erupted about 200 km³ of magma, or 500 km³ of loose material, and left a rock called the Campanian Ignimbrite. Its ash, the Y-5 layer, spread over about 3,000,000 km². It coincided with a suite of biological and cultural changes in and beyond the Mediterranean. One theory blamed it for the Neanderthals' extinction. A 2021 recalibration, however, puts their disappearance at 40,700 ± 200 years ago, before the eruption.

late-066.title: The paintings of Chauvet Cave
late-066.text: Chauvet Cave in southeastern France holds some of the world's best-preserved figurative cave paintings. Its floors also keep remains and prints of animals, some now extinct. Radiocarbon dates show two occupations, 37,000 to 33,500 and 31,000 to 28,000 years ago. Most black drawings belong to the first, and the oldest was painted about 36,500 years ago. About 29,000 years ago a cliff collapsed and sealed the entrance.

late-067.title: Stegodon fades from mainland Asia
late-067.text: Stegodon, an elephant relative, lasted in Asia long after it died out in Africa. It lived across South, Southeast and East Asia. Its last mainland records date to perhaps 35,000 to 30,000 years ago in India and at least 30,000 to 20,000 in China; later claims are unsubstantiated. The harsh Last Glacial Maximum may have contributed. Asian elephants, with more flexible diets, survived. Whether climate, hunting or both caused such losses is debated.

late-068.title: The Gravettian spreads across Europe
late-068.text: Clay fragments at Pavlov I in Moravia bear the impressions of woven textiles, about 26,980 to 24,870 years old. They belong to the Gravettian culture, which succeeded the Aurignacian about 33,000 years ago. It reached as far as Estremadura in Portugal, and Venus figurines are among its hallmarks. It had mostly disappeared by about 22,000 years ago, near the Last Glacial Maximum, though some elements lasted until about 17,000 years ago.

late-069.title: Disputed early sites in the Americas
late-069.text: Did people reach the Americas before the last great ice? Stones from Chiquihuite Cave in Mexico, thought to be tools, are dated to 26,000 years ago and possibly 33,000. Bluefish Caves in the Yukon may record people 24,000 years ago, though the dates are contested. Mammoth bones at Old Crow Flats, apparently butchered, date to 25,000 to 40,000 years ago. Skeptics note that the oldest sites with many artifacts in undisturbed layers, in eastern Beringia, date to 14,200 to 13,000 years ago.

late-070.title: Dogs part ways with wolves
late-070.text: The oldest known dog skeletons, from Siberia's Altai Mountains and a cave in Belgium, date to about 33,000 years ago. Mitochondrial DNA puts the split of dogs from wolves 32,100 to 18,800 years ago, pointing to a European origin among hunter-gatherers. A 2021 review instead places the start of domestication in Siberia, 26,000 to 19,700 years ago, among Ancient North Eurasians. From there dogs spread east and west.

late-071.title: The ancestors of Native Americans reach Beringia
late-071.text: About 36,000 years ago, the ancestors of the first Americans split from Ancient East Asians and moved north into Siberia. They lived as far east as Beringia before 32,000 years ago. Lake sediments in northern Alaska suggest they burned landscapes there as early as 34,000 years ago. Through the Last Glacial Maximum, a population of at most a few thousand lived in Beringia. There, 25,000 to 20,000 years ago, the Ancestral Native American lineage formed.
